paragraphs.text: For most of the history of life on Earth, the loudest sounds were natural ones: thunder, waves, the calls of other animals. Today, the hum of roads, the roar of aircraft and the throb of ship engines reach places that were once almost silent. Because noise leaves no visible trace, it was long treated as a nuisance for people rather than as a form of pollution affecting nature. Yet for a great many animals, hearing is not a minor sense. Birds use song to defend territories and attract partners, bats and dolphins find food by listening to echoes, and many prey species depend on detecting the faint rustle of an approaching predator. When human sound drowns out these signals, the consequences can reach far beyond simple annoyance.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Some of the clearest evidence comes from cities. Researchers have found that several bird species living near busy roads sing at a higher pitch than members of the same species in quieter areas, lifting their songs above the low rumble of traffic. Others simply sing more loudly, a response also seen in humans, who raise their voices in a crowded restaurant without thinking about it. In some cities, robins have been recorded singing at night, when the streets are calmer. These adjustments show that birds can be remarkably flexible, but flexibility is not the same as being unaffected. A higher or louder song may demand more energy, and it may not carry the same information to a listening female as the song it replaced.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Studies like these face a basic problem. A noisy street is also a brightly lit, polluted and heavily built-up one, so it is hard to know whether noise itself is responsible for what scientists observe. To get around this, the field biologist Ottilie Nakamura designed an experiment in a remote woodland with no roads nearby. She placed weatherproof loudspeakers among a group of nest boxes and played recordings of traffic for part of each breeding season, leaving a similar group of boxes undisturbed for comparison. Because the woods were otherwise identical, any difference could be linked to sound alone. In her study, parents nesting near the speakers made fewer feeding visits to their young, apparently spending more time scanning for danger they could no longer hear, and their chicks left the nest at a lower weight. Nakamura is careful to describe the result as a single study of one species, but she argues that the method itself is what matters: it allows noise to be switched on and off like a variable in a laboratory.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Beneath the sea, the problem takes a different form. Sound travels much faster and farther in water than in air, which is why many marine animals rely on it more than on sight. Large whales produce low-frequency calls that can be detected across great distances, but the engines and propellers of cargo ships produce noise in much the same frequency range. As a result, the area over which two whales can hear each other may shrink dramatically when a vessel passes, an effect known as masking. There are signs that the noise causes stress as well. On one occasion when shipping in a busy bay was briefly interrupted, researchers found that levels of stress-related hormones in the droppings of local whales fell noticeably compared with previous years.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Studying animals that may be hundreds of kilometres away and rarely come to the surface requires patience and technology. The marine acoustician Bayo Lindgren fixed a line of underwater microphones, or hydrophones, to the seabed alongside a major shipping lane and left them recording for eighteen months. No team could listen to so much sound, so he trained computer software to pick out whale calls automatically and then matched them against public records of ship movements. His analysis suggested that whales calling while a large ship was nearby repeated their calls more often, as if trying to make sure they were heard. Lindgren points out, however, that hydrophones only record the animals that call; a whale that falls silent in response to noise is invisible to his equipment, so the true effect may be larger than his data show.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Unlike many pollutants, noise has one encouraging feature: it disappears almost as soon as its source is removed. Chemicals can remain in soil and water for decades, but a quiet road is quiet immediately. This means that practical measures can bring rapid benefits. Ships that reduce their speed in sensitive areas produce considerably less underwater noise, and newer propeller designs can make them quieter still. On land, low-noise road surfaces and barriers can reduce disturbance, and construction work can be scheduled to avoid the breeding season. The ecologist Catalina Rourke believes the most important change is a simpler one: recording the natural sounds of a site before any building begins, so that planners know what they stand to lose. As she notes, the quieter places that result are rarely appreciated by wildlife alone.
paragraphs.label: F

section.text:
A Noisier World for Wildlife

A. For most of the history of life on Earth, the loudest sounds were natural ones: thunder, waves, the calls of other animals. Today, the hum of roads, the roar of aircraft and the throb of ship engines reach places that were once almost silent. Because noise leaves no visible trace, it was long treated as a nuisance for people rather than as a form of pollution affecting nature. Yet for a great many animals, hearing is not a minor sense. Birds use song to defend territories and attract partners, bats and dolphins find food by listening to echoes, and many prey species depend on detecting the faint rustle of an approaching predator. When human sound drowns out these signals, the consequences can reach far beyond simple annoyance.

B. Some of the clearest evidence comes from cities. Researchers have found that several bird species living near busy roads sing at a higher pitch than members of the same species in quieter areas, lifting their songs above the low rumble of traffic. Others simply sing more loudly, a response also seen in humans, who raise their voices in a crowded restaurant without thinking about it. In some cities, robins have been recorded singing at night, when the streets are calmer. These adjustments show that birds can be remarkably flexible, but flexibility is not the same as being unaffected. A higher or louder song may demand more energy, and it may not carry the same information to a listening female as the song it replaced.

C. Studies like these face a basic problem. A noisy street is also a brightly lit, polluted and heavily built-up one, so it is hard to know whether noise itself is responsible for what scientists observe. To get around this, the field biologist Ottilie Nakamura designed an experiment in a remote woodland with no roads nearby. She placed weatherproof loudspeakers among a group of nest boxes and played recordings of traffic for part of each breeding season, leaving a similar group of boxes undisturbed for comparison. Because the woods were otherwise identical, any difference could be linked to sound alone. In her study, parents nesting near the speakers made fewer feeding visits to their young, apparently spending more time scanning for danger they could no longer hear, and their chicks left the nest at a lower weight. Nakamura is careful to describe the result as a single study of one species, but she argues that the method itself is what matters: it allows noise to be switched on and off like a variable in a laboratory.

D. Beneath the sea, the problem takes a different form. Sound travels much faster and farther in water than in air, which is why many marine animals rely on it more than on sight. Large whales produce low-frequency calls that can be detected across great distances, but the engines and propellers of cargo ships produce noise in much the same frequency range. As a result, the area over which two whales can hear each other may shrink dramatically when a vessel passes, an effect known as masking. There are signs that the noise causes stress as well. On one occasion when shipping in a busy bay was briefly interrupted, researchers found that levels of stress-related hormones in the droppings of local whales fell noticeably compared with previous years.

E. Studying animals that may be hundreds of kilometres away and rarely come to the surface requires patience and technology. The marine acoustician Bayo Lindgren fixed a line of underwater microphones, or hydrophones, to the seabed alongside a major shipping lane and left them recording for eighteen months. No team could listen to so much sound, so he trained computer software to pick out whale calls automatically and then matched them against public records of ship movements. His analysis suggested that whales calling while a large ship was nearby repeated their calls more often, as if trying to make sure they were heard. Lindgren points out, however, that hydrophones only record the animals that call; a whale that falls silent in response to noise is invisible to his equipment, so the true effect may be larger than his data show.

F. Unlike many pollutants, noise has one encouraging feature: it disappears almost as soon as its source is removed. Chemicals can remain in soil and water for decades, but a quiet road is quiet immediately. This means that practical measures can bring rapid benefits. Ships that reduce their speed in sensitive areas produce considerably less underwater noise, and newer propeller designs can make them quieter still. On land, low-noise road surfaces and barriers can reduce disturbance, and construction work can be scheduled to avoid the breeding season. The ecologist Catalina Rourke believes the most important change is a simpler one: recording the natural sounds of a site before any building begins, so that planners know what they stand to lose. As she notes, the quieter places that result are rarely appreciated by wildlife alone.

explanation.uk: В абзаці B сказано, що птахи здатні пристосовуватися, але це не означає, що шум на них не впливає. З тексту випливає, що змінений спів може вимагати більше енергії, а не менше, а вільшанки співають уночі, бо на вулицях тихіше, а не через освітлення.

options.text: To record traffic noise without any interruption
To exclude factors such as light and pollution
To study a species that is found only in forests
To avoid disturbing birds that nest in cities

questions.prompt: Why did Nakamura carry out her experiment in a remote woodland?
questions.evidence: A noisy street is also a brightly lit, polluted and heavily built-up one

explanation.en: Paragraph C explains that city streets differ in light, pollution and buildings as well as noise. The quiet woodland let Nakamura test the effect of sound alone.
explanation.ru: В абзаце C объясняется, что городские улицы различаются не только шумом, но и освещением, загрязнением и застройкой. Тихий лес позволил Nakamura проверить влияние одного только звука.
explanation.uk: В абзаці C пояснюється, що міські вулиці відрізняються не лише шумом, а й освітленням, забрудненням і забудовою. Тихий ліс дав Nakamura змогу перевірити вплив самого лише звуку.

the tendency of whales to avoid busy shipping lanes.
the shrinking of the range in which whales can communicate.
the stress that whales experience when a vessel passes.

questions.prompt: In paragraph D, the term 'masking' refers to
questions.evidence: the area over which two whales can hear each other may shrink dramatically when a vessel passes, an effect known as masking

explanation.en: Paragraph D defines masking as the reduced area over which whales can hear each other. Stress is mentioned in the next sentence as a separate effect ('as well').
explanation.ru: В абзаце D маскировка определяется как сокращение площади, в пределах которой киты слышат друг друга. Стресс упоминается в следующем предложении как отдельное последствие («as well»).
explanation.uk: В абзаці D маскування визначено як зменшення площі, у межах якої кити чують одне одного. Стрес згадано в наступному реченні як окремий наслідок («as well»).
